extracted.intended_audience: readers or analysts of comic fiction (P. G. Wodehouse / early 20th-century humour)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and characterise the humour-writing techniques and implicit evaluative features illustrated in this excerpt of P. G. Wodehouse's Psmith, Journalist. Focus is on what makes the passage comic (voice, devices, pacing, characterisation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent comic narrator/voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a steady, distinctive narrative voice that delivers humour through ironic, urbane commentary rather than overt explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage uses a gently ironic narrator (e.g., 'Work, the what's-its-name of the thingummy and the thing-um-a-bob of the what d'you-call-it.') who treats absurdity as if it were ordinary, letting the humour arise from tone. Preserve that ironic detachment; avoid switching to straightforward exposition which kills the comic tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan understatement
rubrics_metrics.description: Present outrageous or absurd situations in a calm, underplayed manner so the contrast produces comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psmith's cool, matter-of-fact remarks about violent or ludicrous events ('We should have been done if you hadn't.' / 'This act is going to be a scream from start to finish.') exemplify deadpan delivery. Use flat affect and minimal emotional language when describing extremes to amplify humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witty dialogue and banter
rubrics_metrics.description: Use rapid, well-timed exchanges between characters to generate humour through repartee, retorts, and ironic rejoinders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Much comedy here comes from brisk back-and-forths (e.g., Psmith's repartees with Billy Windsor, Jarvis, Parker). Keep comebacks short, slightly exaggerated, and character-specific. Timing (who speaks when, short interruptions) is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic incongruity (register clash)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create humour by juxtaposing elevated/formal language with coarse/slangy speech or improbable contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the aristocratic 'Comrade' and refined diction applied to hoodlums and East-side cat-fanciers; Psmith's high-flown metaphors contrasted with Jarvis's slang ('Aw chee!', 'Say, what do youse want?'). Exploit mismatch between formality and subject to surprise the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive neologisms and coined terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce playful, slightly absurd invented words or foreign-sounding terms to add comic colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The made-up 'sitz-redacteur' and playful phrases (e.g., 'thingummy', 'what d'you-call-it') are used to comic effect. Coin words that sound plausible in-context but reveal the speaker's character or satirise a trope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running gags and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop recurring jokes or motifs across lines or scenes so repetition increases humour rather than dissipates it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurring references (Comrade titles, cat-obsessions, mentions of Kid Brady, 'fits in kittens') build a cumulative comic effect. Reintroduce motifs with slight variation to reward attentive readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-based humour / eccentric stock types
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on strongly drawn, slightly exaggerated character types whose predictable behaviour produces laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters like the urbane Psmith, the blustering Bat Jarvis, Long Otto the silent scrapper, and Mr. Parker the cad are stock-comic types. Give each a consistent quirk (speech pattern, action) and let humour arise from their interactions and predictable reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurd analogy and simile
rubrics_metrics.description: Use unexpected, whimsical comparisons to create visual or intellectual incongruity that amuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comparing a cat's colour to 'a Neapolitan ice' or Psmith likening himself jokingly to a 'Peruvian Llama.' Favor vivid, slightly outlandish comparisons that catch the reader off-guard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polished formal phrasing to present nonsense
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrap silly ideas in elegant, precise sentences so the formality heightens the silliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psmith's elaborate phrasing describing trivialities ('the subtle joy in the manufacture of the well-formed phrase') treats nonsense with pomp, increasing comic contrast. Keep syntax controlled and ornate while the content remains absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational irony and escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct scenes where the situation's outcome runs counter to characters' expectations, and escalate stakes in unexpected, ludicrous ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the intended rough-house visitors finding armed cat-fanciers, King-sized verbal bravado when physical danger is present, and Billy's ill-timed prison escape. Build set-ups that imply one result, then subvert and escalate for comic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of understatement about violence/slapstick
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe physical mishaps or threats with restrained language or in conversational tones to make them funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violent or slapstick incidents (men cannoning into the table, Psmith's hat being shot through elsewhere in the book) are narrated with minimal alarm, provoking laughter by contrast. Avoid melodrama; let the absurdity be spoken of as routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packed-but-lean scene composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep scenes dense with humorous detail and character beats while maintaining forward motion—little scenic padding, many small jokes per paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The excerpt packs jokes, character quirks, and minor incidents into short stretches (e.g., the Groome Street visit). Prefer tightly written paragraphs filled with distinct comic beats rather than long descriptive detours.
